verses.text: Then he made an altar of brass, twenty cubits  long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.
Also he made the molten sea  of ten cubits from brim to brim. It was round, five cubits high, and thirty cubits in circumference.
Under it was the likeness of oxen, which encircled it, for ten cubits, encircling the sea. The oxen were in two rows, cast when it was cast.

It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; and the sea was set on them above, and all their hindquarters were inward.
It was a handbreadth thick; and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It received and held three thousand baths.

He also made ten basins, and put five on the right hand, and five on the left, to wash in them. The things that belonged to the burnt offering were washed in them; but the sea was for the priests to wash in.
He made the ten lamp stands of gold according to the ordinance concerning them; and he set them in the temple, five on the right hand, and five on the left.
He made also ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right side, and five on the left. He made one hundred basins of gold.
Furthermore he made the court of the priests, the great court, and doors for the court, and overlaid their doors with brass.
He set the sea on the right side of the house eastward, toward the south.
Huram made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Huram finished doing the work that he did for king Solomon in God’s house:
the two pillars, the bowls, the two capitals which were on the top of the pillars, the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars,
and the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks; two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars.
He also made the bases, and he made the basins on the bases;
one sea, and the twelve oxen under it.
Huram his father also made the pots, the shovels, the forks, and all its vessels for king Solomon, for Yahweh’s house, of bright brass.
The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.
Thus Solomon made all these vessels in great abundance; for the weight of the brass could not be determined.
Solomon made all the vessels that were in God’s house, the golden altar also, and the tables with the show bread on them;
and the lamp stands with their lamps, to burn according to the ordinance before the inner sanctuary, of pure gold;
and the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs of gold that was perfect gold;

and the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and the fire pans of pure gold. As for the entry of the house, its inner doors for the most holy place and the doors of the main hall of the temple were of gold.

footnotes.content: Notice the altar's size: twenty by twenty by ten cubits—staggering, unmissable, a declaration that sacrifice matters. The brass, weathered by sun and smoke, would bear the weight of offering after offering. God met His people at altars exactly like this, where they came broken and left covered in grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The molten sea holds three thousand baths—imagine the engineers calculating, the heat required, the molten bronze poured with precision. Yet all that effort serves one quiet purpose: to hold water for washing. Sometimes the grandest labor in God's house is for hidden cleanliness, not glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oxen encircle the sea—not by decoration alone, but cast together with it, ornament and structure woven one. The oxen face outward, as if standing guard over the waters of purification. Strength and service, holding what sustains the sacred work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve oxen hold the sea—one pair for each tribe. Every tribe shares the weight of supporting worship, and every tribe looks toward the four winds. A reminder that God's house belongs to all His people, pointing in all directions from one place of washing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A handbreadth thick—just thick enough to hold, to contain, to last. The brim shaped like a lily bloom speaks of beauty even in utility. Three thousand baths flowed through this vessel, yet it never overflowed or emptied. Such is the supply of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The basins wash the burnt offerings; the sea washes the priests. The offering is cleansed before God; the worshiper is cleansed to draw near. Two kinds of washing, two kinds of preparation. How tender: God ordained both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten golden lampstands, five on each side—symmetry and light filling the temple. Each flame a vigil, a witness, a word without sound saying, 'The Lord watches. He has not slept.' Gold catches the fire and holds it, turning it warm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten tables and one hundred basins of gold—the provision multiplies. Tables for the bread of the presence, basins for holy use, all of gold, all reflecting light. Abundance in God's house is not excess; it is the overflow of care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The court of the priests, the great court, doors overlaid with brass—clear boundaries, sacred space marked and preserved. The priests have a place set apart for their work. Order in worship means order in service, and God honors both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sea placed on the right side of the house, eastward toward the south—every placement deliberate, every measurement sacred. Nothing in the temple hides or clusters; all sits in its appointed station, receiving light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram finished the work—a master craftsman, honored by name, his labor sealed in bronze and gold. He built for 'God's house,' not a wage alone, but for the place where heaven touches earth. His hands knew they served the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pillars, bowls, capitals, networks—each piece named, each piece counted. The listing speaks of care, of completeness, of a work where nothing was left to chance or guesswork. God's house is built with precision and love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four hundred pomegranates for the networks—abundance beyond necessity, every inch adorned. Pomegranates held meaning in Israel: fruitfulness, blessing, life. Solomon's temple says with every detail: this house holds life, blessing, and the very presence of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bases and basins on the bases—form and function, structure and service. Nothing sits unanchored in God's house. Every vessel rests on what supports it; every offering depends on what holds it. Order reflects holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One sea and the twelve oxen under it—all that we saw described earlier now summarized, complete. The mind returns to the image: twelve tribes, one sacred vessel, strength beneath the waters of purification.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram's father—also a craftsman, also named and remembered. He made the smaller vessels, the pots and shovels and forks, all of bright brass. The work of God's house includes both the grand and the humble, both the seen and the necessary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plain of the Jordan, between Succoth and Zeredah—a place named, marked by distance, where the casting happened. The furnishings for God's house emerged from earth and fire in a specific, traceable place. Even the location matters in the story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The weight of the brass could not be determined—abundance so great it surpasses counting, provision so lavish it overwhelms measure. Solomon spared nothing for his God's house. How we build what we love reveals what we treasure most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The golden altar, the tables with showbread—heart and sustenance of worship gathered in one image. The altar receives prayer and offering; the table receives the bread of God's presence. Both speak that He desires our devotion and meets our hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lampstands with lamps to burn according to ordinance—not random, not according to whim, but by God's design, to burn before the inner sanctuary. The fire knows its order; the light knows its purpose. We walk straighter when we follow His ordinance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flowers, lamps, tongs of perfect gold—even the tools, even the small implements, crafted of the finest metal. God's work is done with what is perfect, not what is merely sufficient. The intention of excellence runs through every detail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Snuffers, basins, spoons, fire pans, the doors of gold—the final roll call of vessels, and the sanctuary itself adorned with gold. Looking back from a longer road, we see how God's house holds both the instruments of service and the symbol of His glory. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord still seeks people willing to make their lives vessels of His light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
